name: Cactus
description: A connected undirected graph is called a vertex cactus , if each vertex of this graph belongs to at most one simple cycle. A simple cycle in a undirected graph is a sequence of distinct vertices v 1 , v 2 , ..., v t ( t > 2) , such that for any i (1 ≤ i < t ) exists an edge between vertices v i and v i + 1 , and also exists an edge between vertices v 1 and v t . A simple path in a undirected graph is a sequence of not necessarily distinct vertices v 1 , v 2 , ..., v t ( t > 0) , such that for any i (1 ≤ i < t ) exists an edge between vertices v i and v i + 1 and furthermore each edge occurs no more than once . We'll say that a simple path v 1 , v 2 , ..., v t starts at vertex v 1 and ends at vertex v t . You've got a graph consisting of n vertices and m edges, that is a vertex cactus. Also, you've got a list of k pairs of interesting vertices x i , y i , for which you want to know the following information — the number of distinct simple paths that start at vertex x i and end at vertex y i . We will consider two simple paths distinct if the sets of edges of the paths are distinct. For each pair of interesting vertices count the number of distinct simple paths between them. As this number can be rather large, you should calculate it modulo 1000000007 ( 10 9 + 7 ).
input_specification: The first line contains two space-separated integers n , m (2 ≤ n ≤ 10 5 ; 1 ≤ m ≤ 10 5 ) — the number of vertices and edges in the graph, correspondingly. Next m lines contain the description of the edges: the i -th line contains two space-separated integers a i , b i (1 ≤ a i , b i ≤ n ) — the indexes of the vertices connected by the i -th edge. The next line contains a single integer k (1 ≤ k ≤ 10 5 ) — the number of pairs of interesting vertices. Next k lines contain the list of pairs of interesting vertices: the i -th line contains two space-separated numbers x i , y i (1 ≤ x i , y i ≤ n ; x i ≠ y i ) — the indexes of interesting vertices in the i -th pair. It is guaranteed that the given graph is a vertex cactus. It is guaranteed that the graph contains no loops or multiple edges. Consider the graph vertices are numbered from 1 to n .
output_specification: Print k lines: in the i -th line print a single integer — the number of distinct simple ways, starting at x i and ending at y i , modulo 1000000007 ( 10 9 + 7 ).
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 231E — Cactus [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
